statement: Over 21 million renter households, 49.7% of the 42.5 million for whom rent burden is calculated, spent more than 30% of income on housing costs in 2023.

statement: HUD counts a household as cost-burdened above 30% of income on housing and severely cost-burdened above 50%.
anchor: Households are considered cost-burdened when they spend more than 30% of their income on rent, mortgage payments, and other housing costs, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Households spending more than 50% of their income on housing costs are considered severely cost-burdened.

statement: There were 13.77 million unassisted very low-income renter households in 2023, and 61.4 percent of them had worst case needs.

statement: HUD's latest worst case needs report attributes the elevated needs to wage growth too weak to make rent affordable for low-income renters and to sustained rental demand, which it ties to record immigration.
anchor:
This year’s report shows two realities. The first is that economic growth has been insufficient to
lift the wages of low-income renting families high enough to make rent affordable. The second is
that national macroeconomic policies, such as record immigration, have combined to drive
sustained high rental demand, which has continued to place upward pressure on rent prices.
context: Published July 2025, during the second Trump administration. The report's immigration section rests on research it summarizes on immigration and metropolitan rents; its footnote lists Camarota (1998), Edo (2015), Mussa et al. (2017), Myers et al. (2006), Orrenius and Zavodny (2007) and Saiz (2007), the last a peer-reviewed study of immigration and rents. The report's own decomposition (EV-HOU-029) attributes 321,000 added cases to household formation, which it describes as largely driven by immigration and declining marriage, but does not measure immigration on its own. Its counts come from HUD tabulations of the American Housing Survey and are treated as data (EV-HOU-020 to 024); this causal reading needs independent research before the dossier relies on it.

statement: HUD's 2024 homelessness report names several likely causes of the record count: the affordable housing crisis, inflation, stagnating wages, systemic racism, public health crises, natural disasters, immigration, and the end of pandemic-era prevention programs including the expanded child tax credit.
anchor:
Our worsening national affordable housing crisis, rising inflation, stagnating wages among
middle- and lower-income households, and the persisting effects of systemic racism have stretched
homelessness services systems to their limits. Additional public health crises, natural disasters that
displaced people from their homes, rising numbers of people immigrating to the U.S., and the end to
homelessness prevention programs put in place during the COVID-19 pandemic, including the end of the
expanded child tax credit, have exacerbated this already stressed system.
context: Published December 2024 under the Biden administration. The list of factors is the report's interpretation, offered without estimates of how much each contributed.

statement: HUD's decomposition of the 2021-2023 change in worst case needs: household formation (4.73 million new households), which the report describes as largely driven by record immigration and a long-term decline in marriage rates, added an estimated 321,000 cases, the largest upward demographic factor; a shift toward homeownership removed 247,000, rising renter incomes 163,000 and a narrower rental assistance gap 169,000, so the four demographic factors together reduced needs by 258,000; a tight rental market added 196,000.

Of the four demographic factors, national household formation, largely driven by record levels of
immigration and a continued long-term decline in marriage rates, would have been expected to
increase worst case needs by 321,000 cases. A shift from renting to homeownership diminished
that effect by an estimated 247,000 cases. Improvement in renter incomes accounted for a further

context: The report's quantified analysis (a shift-share decomposition of American Housing Survey estimates). It folds immigration into household formation together with declining marriage rates and does not estimate immigration's share on its own. Household formation is the largest upward demographic factor; homeownership, incomes and assistance more than offset it. So the analysis is consistent with immigration adding to needs, without measuring how much.
